newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: France stakes out territory for future EMU battles.
newsitem.headline: France stakes out territory for future EMU battles.

text.p: France's finance minister, staking out the territory for future battles in Europe, said on Monday an "economic pillar" balancing the "monetary pillar" in monetary union was extremely important to France.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn said that although France's new Socialist-led administration had dropped the label "economic government" it called for in its election campaign, it believed an economic pillar was vital to make the euro a success.
Its call for an economic government fuelled deep anxiety in Germany which fears any political interference which might undermine the independence of the future European Central Bank.
Strauss-Kahn said during an EU summit here that work was only just beginning on the creation of an economic pillar to balance the monetary pillar represented by the independent European central bank.

"This is extremely important for us," he told reporters, adding that first steps taken in this direction at the Amsterdam summit were more significant than a string of measures agreed by EU leaders designed to boost employment.
"The creation of an economic pillar is much more important."

EU leaders agreed to study ways of implementing Article 109 of the Maastricht treaty "on the possible formulation of general orientations for exchange rate policy in relation to one or more non-Community currencies," according to summit conclusions.

This would be "without prejudice to the primary objective of the European System of Central Banks to maintain price stability while fully respecting the statutes of the European Central Bank," the conclusions said.

Strauss-Kahn said France wanted Maastricht treaty provisions for economic policy coordination spelled out in exactly the same way that a "stability pact" limiting budget deficits under EMU fleshed out provisions prohibiting big deficits.
EU leaders agreed on Monday on the stability pact, proposed by Germany to ensure Economic and Monetary Union is underpinned by sound budgetary policies.

Strauss-Kahn said there could be an initial report on the creation of an economic pillar during the next six months when Luxembourg will hold the EU's rotating presidency, followed by a resolution in the following six months.
"An economic pillar is essential for the success of the euro," he said.
France's previous centre-right government had pushed hard for a "stability council" to coordinate economic policies in euro zone.

After initially running into resistance from Germany, notably its powerful Bundesbank, France finally settled for an accord on an informal stability council which would have no real power to set policy.
Strauss-Kahn, however, said the stability council was only a first step in the direction of creating the economic pillar.
"It was a first step, but a very modest one," he said.
He said the EU would have to look at intensifying "coordination in all areas including exchange rates".
This would include, for example, deciding who would represent the euro zone at international meetings, he said.
Strauss-Kahn did not say how governments and the future European Central Bank would share out responsibility for exchange rate policy.
For Germany, the principle of non-interference by politicians in exchange rates is virtually sacrosanct.
But France has traditionally seen exchange rate policy as a normal part of economic policy.
The Socialist party said in its election campaign it would fight for a euro which was not overvalued against the dollar.
Strauss-Kahn said the current rate between the dollar and European currencies was not a problem -- at least at the moment -- given the recent rise in the dollar.
